_about: Single source of truth for every rendering, and the auditable term ledger (check 5). ONE rendering per referent for the whole book. Before you romanize any name, check here AND authority.json (the cross-book ledger). status per entry: 'attested' (form used in English scholarship, give the citation in note), 'provisional' (your romanization, not found in outside sources), 'decided' (a project style call). Keys starting with '_' are ignored. Seeded at the survey from authority.json; enriched per batch. Bylines/contributors are added as each article is translated.

杜月笙.cast: 1888–1951; the foremost of Shanghai's ‘three big bosses,’ a Green Gang chief who rose from a fruit-stall boy to a power broker between the underworld, the concessions and the Nationalist state. The subject of seven articles here.
杜月笙.note: 1888–1951. Foremost of the Shanghai Green Gang ‘three tycoons.’ Pinyin form standard across the collection.

黄金荣.cast: 1868–1953; the senior of the three bosses, and the only Chinese chief detective of the French Concession police. Three articles here.
黄金荣.note: Green Gang boss and the sole Chinese chief inspector of the French Concession detective squad; Chiang Kai-shek was once nominally his disciple.

张啸林.cast: 1877–1940; the third of the three bosses, a Hangzhou-born strongman; later a collaborator with the Japanese, assassinated in 1940.
张啸林.note: One of the ‘three big bosses’ of the Shanghai gangs, with Huang Jinrong and Du Yuesheng.

顾竹轩.cast: b. 1885; Green Gang boss of the Zhabei district, rickshaw-fleet magnate and owner of the Tianchan Stage; sheltered Communist underground workers.
顾竹轩.note: Jiangsu-born gang figure who dominated Zhabei; two articles here treat his rise and his cover for revolutionary work.

张仁奎.cast: 1865–1944; a senior Green Gang master of the ‘Big’ (Da) generation whose disciples filled Shanghai; founder of the Ren Society.
张仁奎.note: Elder Green Gang figure; Du Yuesheng and many others were ranked below his generation.

戴笠.cast: 1897–1946; head of the Nationalists' secret service (the Juntong); Du Yuesheng's wartime partner.
戴笠.note: Head of the Nationalists' Bureau of Investigation and Statistics (军统/Juntong), the KMT secret police.

朱学范.note: 1905–1996; postal-workers’ leader who rose through the Green Gang and the Nationalist labour apparatus, broke with the Kuomintang in 1948, and became a minister and vice-chairman of the NPC Standing Committee in the People’s Republic. Author of this article and calligrapher of the book’s title.

陆京士.note: d. 1975; Du Yuesheng’s foremost disciple in the labour world, boss of the postal union and a Nationalist party and Garrison Command official; the author’s colleague and rival. Followed the Kuomintang to Taiwan.

李立三.note: 1899–1967; early Communist labour organizer, a leader of the May Thirtieth Movement and briefly the Party’s top leader (the ‘Li Lisan line,’ 1930).

杨度.note: 1875–1931; classical scholar who championed constitutional monarchy under Yuan Shikai, then reinvented himself—joining the Communist Party in secret in 1929 while serving as an adviser to Du Yuesheng. His CCP membership was made public only in 1975.

李大钊.note: 1889–1927; co-founder of the Chinese Communist Party. Seized from the Soviet embassy in Beijing and hanged on Zhang Zuolin’s orders in April 1927.

赵朴初.note: 1907–2000; Buddhist lay leader, poet, and relief organizer; secretly aided the Communist underground through Shanghai’s charitable and refugee bodies in the war years, and later headed the Buddhist Association of China.

闻兰亭.note: Green Gang figure prominent in Shanghai commercial and charitable circles; used by the underground through the wartime relief committees, later pressed into a puppet commercial-control post.

向海潜.note: 1888–1974; also called Xiang Songpo; a leader of the Hongmen (the ‘Five Lakes’ lodges) and a veteran of the 1911 Revolution.

张克昌.note: Postal-union gangster and the author’s fellow disciple under Du Yuesheng; founder of the Chang Society (畅社), who went over to the puppet Wang Jingwei regime as a deputy minister.

金廷荪.note: Green Gang figure and Du Yuesheng associate; patron of the Ming Society (铭社), one of the disciple-societies modelled on Du’s Heng Society.

章士钊.note: 1881–1973; scholar, lawyer, and sometime Beiyang education minister who named Du Yuesheng’s Heng Society; later a noted public figure in the People’s Republic.

汪精卫.note: 1883–1944; senior Nationalist leader who in 1938 defected to Japan and headed the collaborationist ‘reorganized’ government at Nanjing; his name is a byword in these pages for the puppet regime.

吴成方.note: Author of this article; a Communist underground organizer who ran united-front work with gang and secret-society figures in Beijing and Shanghai from the 1920s to the 1940s.

胡鄂公.note: 1884–1951; also known as Hu Nanhu; a 1911 revolutionary and Beiyang official who joined the Communist Party in the 1920s and worked the united front among old revolutionaries and gang figures.

翁文灏.note: 1889–1971; geologist and Nationalist official, acting president of Tsinghua University in 1931 and later premier; returned to the mainland in 1951.

冯玉祥.note: 1882–1948; the ‘Christian general,’ a warlord who at times allied with the Nationalists, the Soviets, and the left; organized the short-lived Chahar People’s Anti-Japanese Allied Army in 1933.

李世瑜.note: 1922–2010; folklorist and historian of Chinese popular religion and secret societies, author of this study of the Green Gang.

姜豪.note: The author of the second study; a Baoshan-born Kuomintang figure and initiated Green Gang member of the ‘Da’ generation who writes here partly from the inside.

金幼孜.note: The gang legend’s ‘first patriarch.’ A real Ming official (1368–1431), Grand Secretary under the Yongle emperor; the gang genealogy built around him is legend.

罗清.note: The gang legend’s ‘second patriarch,’ conflated with Patriarch Luo, founder of the Luo (Non-Action) sect.

潘清.note: Of the three founder-patriarchs, Pan is reckoned the chief; Green Gang men called one another ‘the Pan brothers.’

王伦.note: d. 1774; leader of the Clear Water sect (a White Lotus offshoot) whose 1774 rising at Linqing drew on the grain-transport boatmen.

杨虎.note: Also named Xiaotian; Songhu garrison commander and Green Gang figure.

向松坡.note: Xiang Haiqian; see the note at his first appearance.

薛耕莘.note: The author of this chapter; the byline prints the variant graph 畊 for 耕.

川岛芳子.note: See the note at her first appearance.

袁寒云.cast: 1889–1931; the poet, collector and Green Gang celebrity Yuan Kewen, second son of Yuan Shikai, who opposed his father's monarchy. The subject of ch10, told by his disciple Chen Timin.
袁寒云.note: Yuan Kewen (袁克文), hao Hanyun; pinyin form used across the collection.

程锡文.note: Narrator of ch13; Huang Jinrong’s household steward, who tells the family from the inside.

杨展成.note: Recorder who set down Cheng Xiwen’s ch13 account.

黄振世.note: Narrator of ch14; a fishery-company manager, Huang disciple and later a standing director of the Rong Society, who writes as a self-confessed insider.

何国涛.note: Recorder who set down Huang Zhenshi’s ch14 account.

林桂生.note: Huang Jinrong’s first wife as named in ch13; a formidable figure in her own right. ch14 and later scholarship give her surname as Lin; the source’s own editors flag the variant Ye Guisheng. See the note at ch14.

叶桂生.note: Huang Jinrong’s first wife as named by the ch14 narrator; the source’s editors add that one account gives her as Lin Guisheng (so ch13). Rendered as each narrator prints; the discrepancy is footnoted.

范开泰.note: “Ebony Kaitai,” a City God Temple man about town and temple director; his wife was Shi Jinxiu.

史锦绣.note: “Bandit Jinxiu,” a formidable Changzhou woman of the City God Temple demi-monde, sworn sister to Huang’s first wife.

范回春.note: Younger brother of Fan Kaitai; a bank manager and deputy manager of the Sanxin opium combine.

徐福生.note: “Havoc-in-Heaven Fusheng,” a Suzhou-Creek wharf hoodlum and Huang disciple, said to have introduced Huang Jinrong to Sun Yat-sen.

张方庚.note: A Huang disciple who ran the Dacheng leather-goods company.

韩荣浦.note: A Wu Peifu adjutant whose stray tip, in Huang’s telling, cracked the Bishop Yao kidnapping; later a go-between to Yuan Kewen.

马雨亭.note: A Huang disciple skilled at making rigged gambling gear.

徐阿东.note: The French police hoodlum-squad foreman whom Huang and Du brought to heel, a turning point in the men-about-town’s rise.

陈培德.note: Huang Jinrong’s favored disciple, a British-American Tobacco union chairman; his arrest by Du Yuesheng’s man Lu Jingshi sharpened the Huang–Du feud.

陈福康.note: Manager of the Huang household’s real estate and the Great World accounts; head of a rival clique to the narrator within Huang’s gate.

邱子嘉.note: Works manager of the Renfeng mill and a core Zhongxin/Rong Society organizer allied with the narrator.

王兴高.note: The Subei disciple of Gu Zhuxuan who shot Tang Jiapeng dead at the Great World gate.

周信芳.note: 1895–1975; the great Peking-opera actor known by his stage name Qilintong (麒麟童), who took Huang Jinrong as master for protection against Gu Zhuxuan.

常春恒.note: A wenwu-laosheng Peking-opera actor beaten to death on Gu Zhuxuan’s order in a salary dispute at the Tianchan Stage.

吴世宝.note: “Killer Taibao,” guard chief of the Japanese puppet secret service at No. 76 Jessfield Road; his open threats cowed even the concession detective-chiefs.

余爱珍.note: Wife of Wu Shibao; the shooting of her bodyguard by a Settlement constable in May 1941 was a notorious “76” incident.

潘七分.note: Styled Zixin (子欣); a Tianjin gang chief in Huang’s wide network. Huang trusted him in his last years and called him “Old Seventh Pan.” The ch14 narrator prints his name both as Pan Qifen and, at his first mention, Pan Zixin.

潘子欣.note: See Pan Qifen; the Tianjin gang chief is named both ways in ch14, rendered as printed.

杭州阿法.note: A grand hoodlum of the early Republic raised up by Huang Jinrong, who monopolized opium delivery on the Shiliupu wharves; the source notes a variant graph 阿发.

马鸿魁.note: The “Night-soil King” of the French Concession, a Huang disciple. Not the Ningxia warlord Ma Hongkui (马鸿逵).

唐嘉鹏.note: Manager of the Great World and one of the two great pillars of Huang’s gate; murdered in the feud with Gu Zhuxuan’s faction.

丁永昌.note: A trusted Huang disciple who ran the Great World and carried out kidnappings for him.

鲁锦臣.note: A close Huang disciple and French-police detective-chief who attended the old man in his retirement.

庞京周.note: A prominent Shanghai physician, Du Yuesheng's personal doctor.

李祖夔.note: A former magistrate of Shanghai county.

陈布雷.note: 1890–1948; Chiang Kai-shek's confidential secretary and chief speechwriter.

吴稚晖.note: 1865–1953; veteran Kuomintang elder and calligrapher; also written 吴敬恒.

吴敬恒.note: The formal given name of the Kuomintang elder better known by his courtesy name, Wu Zhihui; the same man.

唐绍仪.note: 1862–1938; first premier of the Republic; assassinated in Shanghai after contacts with the Japanese.

高宗武.note: A Nationalist diplomat active in the secret peace talks with Japan that led to Wang Jingwei's defection.

杨杰.note: 1889–1949; Nationalist general who turned against Chiang; assassinated by Juntong agents on the eve of the Communist victory.

吴开先.note: A leading member of the CC Clique in Shanghai.

胡宗南.note: 1896–1962; the Nationalist general who commanded the northwest.

朱子桥.note: General Zhu Qinglan, a noted relief philanthropist of the Republican era.

张嘉璈.note: Chang Kia-ngau (1889–1979), the banker and financial administrator.

梅乐斯.note: 1900–1961; U.S. Navy officer, head of the American side of the Sino-American Cooperation Organization.

王新衡.note: A Juntong department head and Du Yuesheng's channel to Dai Li.

吴绍澍.note: Du's disciple turned rival; postwar vice-mayor of Shanghai who publicly broke with him.

毛人凤.note: Dai Li's successor as head of the Baomiju secret service.

蒋经国.note: 1910–1988; Chiang Kai-shek's elder son, later president of the Republic of China on Taiwan; here the enforcer of the 1948 gold-yuan reform in Shanghai.

孔令侃.note: H. H. Kung's son and chairman of the Yangtze Company; Chiang Ching-kuo's cousin.

宋美龄.note: 1898–2003; Madame Chiang Kai-shek, sister of T. V. Soong and aunt of Kong Lingkan.

方治.note: A CC Clique figure; chairman of the Shanghai municipal party headquarters.

俞飞鹏.note: A Chiang confidant who headed wartime transport.

青帮.note: 青帮; the great secret-society brotherhood of the lower Yangtze and Shanghai. Rendered ‘Green Gang’ across the collection.

洪门.note: 洪门; the sworn-brotherhood secret society of south China (the ‘Red Gang,’ 洪帮). Kept as Hongmen across the collection.

恒社.note: 恒社; Du Yuesheng's mutual-aid society, founded 1932, through which he organized his following. Its charter and 1934 member roll are the book's appendices.

仁社.note: 仁社; the society founded around the elder gang master Zhang Renkui, a counterpart to Du Yuesheng's Heng Society.

军统.note: 军统; the Nationalists' Bureau of Investigation and Statistics (secret service). Cross-shelf rendering is unsettled (Military Statistics Bureau / the Juntong); this book's rendering is decided at the batch that translates ch21 and reconciled into authority.json then.

毅社.note: 毅社; the disciple-society the author founded in 1934–36 among Shanghai unionists, modelled on Du Yuesheng’s Heng Society; its emblem punned on the author’s name, Zhu Xuefan.

畅社.note: 畅社; the rival postal disciple-society founded by Zhang Kechang.

别动队.note: 别动队; the irregular units raised from Green Gang and Hongmen men during the 1937 Battle of Shanghai, armed and run in connection with Dai Li’s secret service.

天地会.note: The Tiandihui, the great anti-Qing sworn-brotherhood movement of south China, aiming to ‘overthrow the Qing and restore the Ming’; part of the Hongmen tradition.

安庆道友会.note: The Anqing Daoyou Hui, rendered ‘the Anqing Fellowship of the Way’; the fuller early form of the Green Gang, from which the names An-Qing Gang, Clear Gang, and Green Gang evolved.

荣社.note: Huang Jinrong’s disciple-organization, its name taken from his.

忠义救国军.note: A Dai Li / Juntong-affiliated irregular force active in the lower Yangtze during the war.

致公堂.note: The overseas Hongmen lodge network; Cantonese romanization.

忠信社.note: “Loyalty and Faith” Society; the disciple-society Huang Jinrong let his men form in 1936 to undermine Du Yuesheng’s Heng Society. Named from the “learning, conduct, loyalty, faith” tablet in Chiang Kai-shek’s hand at the Huang garden; revived after the war as the Rong Society.

益社.note: The disciple-fraternity Fan Shaozeng, this chapter's narrator, ran in Shanghai on the model of Du Yuesheng's Heng Society.

港济公司.note: The opium-trafficking front company Du set up with Dai Li in 1939, with offices in Chongqing and Hong Kong, nominally under Gu Jiatang.

通济公司.note: The wartime trading company (c. 1943) fronted by Du for Dai Li, smuggling goods to and from the occupied areas under cover of Juntong privilege.

扬子公司.note: Kong Lingkan's Shanghai firm, a byword for wartime and postwar profiteering under the protection of H. H. Kung.

保密局.note: The Bureau of Confidential Affairs, the 1946 renaming of the Juntong secret service.

帮会.note: 帮会; the secret-society brotherhoods (青帮 and 洪门) collectively — the book's subject. Rendered ‘the gangs’ or ‘the secret-society gangs’ as context needs; the title's 帮会 is ‘Gangs.’

通草.note: The gang’s internal secret handbooks (通草, also written 通潦, 通钮, or 统抄), recording the patriarchs, the boat system, gang rules, ritual, and argot; kept provisional as no standard English form is attested.

香堂.note: The xiangtang, the altar-hall where initiations and gang rites were held, before the spirit-tablets of the patriarchs.

青皮.note: Literally ‘green skin’; a term for a bold local tough, one proposed origin of the name ‘Green Gang.’

海底.note: The Hongmen's book of rules and ritual.
